title: ProximalFM: Amortized Proximal Causal Inference under Hidden Confounding

paper.title: ProximalFM : Amortized Proximal Causal Inference under Hidden Confounding
paper.abstract: Abstract Standard causal identification methods often assume no unmeasured confounding and can fail when relevant confounders are unobserved. Proximal causal inference instead uses proxy variables to identify effects under hidden confounding and additional assumptions. However, nonparametric proximal estimation can be challenging in practice: recovering causal estimands such as the conditional average treatment effect (CATE) requires solving an ill-posed integral equation that is data-hungry, hyperparameter-sensitive, and optimization-unstable. Bayesian inference for such models provides a desirable alternative, mitigating these difficulties by regularizing through the prior. However, computing a posterior is itself challenging, as a typical likelihood function will include latent variables. Following the recent success of tabular foundation models in backdoor, instrumental variable, and frontdoor settings, we propose that prior-data fitted networks (PFNs) are uniquely suited to resolve this bottleneck. Indeed, by training on synthetic data sampled from compliant structural causal models with access to oracle counterfactuals, we simplify the task substantially, amortizing the implied Bayesian operator inversion into a single transformer forward pass. Compared to prior literature that focuses primarily on point estimation, our model, ProximalFM , explicitly targets the Bayesian posterior distribution of the CATE. One unique aspect of this problem is that we need to provide Monte Carlo estimates of the oracle CATEs, leading to a novel variation of PFNs that accounts for the added stochastic error. Across a diverse suite of proximal regimes, ProximalFM achieves consistently strong CATE-estimation performance without dataset-specific tuning, with its largest advantage when latent confounding is substantial and the proxies are weakly informative; it also provides fast inference through a single amortized forward pass.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Causal inference from observational data is a fundamental task across disciplines, yet its validity typically hinges on the no unmeasured confounding assumption . This assumption requires that investigators have measured a sufficiently rich set of covariates to ensure that supervised regression and classification functions can, in theory, also provide how an outcome varies under intervention on a possible cause of interest ( Hernán and Robins, 2020 ) , with specialized estimation methods improving on off-the-shelf uses of supervised learning. In practice, however, there are often unmeasured variables that are plausible confounders (e.g., unrecorded disease severity). One of the most common tasks in causal inference is estimating the conditional average treatment effect (CATE) function: how an outcome variable Y Y potentially varies in expectation, as we vary a treatment variable A A by intervening on the latter. This is a function of an observed realization of a vector of covariates X X . Using the notation Y ⁡ ( a ) Y(a) to denote the potential outcome under a hypothetical intervention on A A at level a a ( Rubin, 1972 ) , the CATE function for a binary A A is given by Q ⁡ ( x ) = 𝔼 ⁡ [ Y ⁡ ( 1 ) − Y ⁡ ( 0 ) ∣ X = x ] . Q(x)=\mathbb{E}[Y(1)-Y(0)\mid X=x]. (1) This is identifiable from observational data if unconfoundedness holds. That failing, other assumptions are needed. Proximal causal learning has emerged as a principled framework to identify and estimate causal effects when hidden confounders cannot be ruled out ( Tchetgen Tchetgen et al., 2020 ) . The main idea is to exploit auxiliary variables, proxies , which are associated with the hidden confounders without fully removing their influence. However, using proxy information while avoiding parametric models requires solving ill-posed integral equations, leading to a difficult estimation problem. As a result, current nonparametric ( Ghassami et al., 2022 ; Sverdrup and Cui, 2023 ; Yang et al., 2023 ) and neural estimation methods (NMMR, Kompa et al., 2022 ) are computationally demanding, requiring intensive, dataset-specific optimization. Simultaneously, the machine learning community is shifting toward amortized inference via foundation models. Prior-data fitted networks (PFNs, Müller et al., 2022 ) have demonstrated that transformers can learn to perform Bayesian inference through in-context learning. Models like TabPFN and its successors have shown state-of-the-art performance on small tabular datasets without requiring retraining ( Grinsztajn et al., 2026 ) . As we review in the next section, recent work has extended PFN-style models to causal inference settings. However, they generally do not make use of proximal assumptions, limiting their utility in the presence of hidden confounders. Our contributions are: 1. ProximalFM : a foundation model for proximal causal learning. We introduce ProximalFM , the first tabular foundation model designed for proximal causal inference. It leverages proxy variables without requiring dataset-specific training at deployment. Causal effects are obtained in a single forward pass through a target dataset, providing a Bayesian solution to an ill-posed inverse problem without hyperparameter tuning. 2. A structural prior and Monte Carlo CATE targets for proximal causal learning. We introduce a diverse prior over structural causal models that enforces the proximal assumptions for identification. We use Monte Carlo integration to approximate the CATE. These approximations are then used as targets to train ProximalFM . This prior determines the inductive bias regularizing the proximal estimation problem amortized by ProximalFM . 3. Comprehensive evaluation, from semi-synthetic data to physical systems. We evaluate ProximalFM on diverse semi-synthetic proximal benchmarks that combine real-world covariate distributions with known, controlled causal mechanisms. Beyond semi-synthetic benchmarks, we take a first step towards evaluation on real physical systems using Causal Chambers ( Gamella et al., 2025 ) , a controlled physical testbed for causal inference.

sections.heading: Tabular foundation models
sections.text: Recent advances have demonstrated the potential of transformer-based foundation models for tabular prediction. TabPFN pioneered this approach for supervised learning tasks with tabular data ( Hollmann et al., 2023 ; Hollmann et al., 2025 ; Grinsztajn et al., 2026 ) . This success prompted a rapidly expanding literature. Examples include work on more efficient tabular in-context learning, such as TabICL ( Qu et al., 2025 ; Qu et al., 2026 ) , and tuning on real-world data, as in RealTabPFN ( Garg et al., 2025 ) . This progress has also motivated standardized evaluation. TabArena provides a living benchmark for IID tabular classification and regression ( Erickson et al., 2026 ) . Extending this evaluation beyond conventional IID settings, Purucker et al. (2026) find that current tabular foundation models are particularly strong on small- to medium-scale IID datasets, but do not yet consistently outperform conventional methods on non-IID, large-scale, or high-dimensional data.

sections.heading: Amortized causal learning
sections.text: The success of tabular models has motivated their application to causal inference. Causal foundation models are pretrained on a prior over causal data-generating processes and use in-context learning to estimate causal quantities on new datasets in a single forward pass. Stith et al. (2026b) provide a recent overview of this emerging literature. Robertson et al. (2026) introduced Do-PFN, demonstrating that transformer-based foundation models can learn causal estimation procedures directly from synthetic data and perform zero-shot inference on unseen datasets. Balazadeh Meresht et al. (2026) introduced CausalPFN, a framework for doing amortized learning of causal effects identified through unconfoundedness. This setting was also considered in Luedtke and Chung (2024) , under an adversarially chosen prior. Ma et al. (2026) proposed CausalFM, extending causal foundation models beyond unconfoundedness, such as the case of identifiable additive-error instrumental-variable (IV) settings. Rather than learning a single causal estimator, CausalFM trains separate models for distinct causal identification strategies, thereby preserving the classical separation between identification and estimation. Balazadeh et al. (2026) relaxes the assumption of additive-error in the IV setting to build in-context learners for bounding causal effects for instrumental variables. Different from proximal learning, such partial identification IV methods do not typically exploit multiple proxies, nor exploit completeness assumptions (as defined in the next section) that could otherwise allow for identification. Despite these advances, a foundation model designed for proximal causal inference remains absent from the literature.

sections.heading: 2 Proximal causal inference
sections.text: We consider an observational causal inference setting where the standard assumption of no unmeasured fails. Our objective is to estimate the CATE, as in Eq. ( 1 ), for binary treatments. Let the observed variables be O = ( L , A , Y ) O=(L,A,Y) , where A ∈ { 0 , 1 } A\in\{0,1\} denotes a treatment of interest, Y Y is the outcome, and L L is a set of measured covariates. The unmeasured confounders are denoted by U U . In the presence of U U , the standard exchangeability condition Y ⁡ ( a ) ⟂ ⟂ A | L Y(a)\perp\!\!\!\perp A\mid L is violated ( Hernán and Robins, 2020 ) . To achieve identification, we adopt the proximal causal learning framework (see, e.g., Miao et al., 2018 ; Tchetgen Tchetgen et al., 2020 ) . This framework partitions L L into three subsets, each with a distinct role. Let L = ( X , Z , W ) L=(X,Z,W) where X X contains baseline covariates, while Z Z and W W are complementary proxies for U U . Z Z is a treatment-confounding proxy: while it carries information about the latent U U , it may otherwise be related directly to treatment assignment. Conversely, W W is an outcome-confounding proxy which carries information about U U and may otherwise directly shape the outcome. sections.heading: 2.2 Classical and modern estimation via bridge functions
sections.text: In addition to Assumptions 1 – 4 , we assume the regularity conditions ensuring the existence of an outcome confounding bridge function h 0 ​ ( W , A , X ) h_{0}(W,A,X) . This function satisfies the Fredholm integral equation ( Miao et al., 2018 ; Tchetgen Tchetgen et al., 2020 ) 𝔼 [ Y ∣ Z , A , X ] = 𝔼 [ h 0 ( W , A , X ) ∣ Z , A , X ] . \mathbb{E}[Y\mid Z,A,X]=\mathbb{E}[h_{0}(W,A,X)\mid Z,A,X]. (2) The bridge function enables identification of the conditional average treatment effect through the proximal g-formula Q ⁡ ( x ) = 𝔼 ⁡ [ h 0 ​ ( W , 1 , X ) − h 0 ​ ( W , 0 , X ) ∣ X = x ] . Q(x)=\mathbb{E}[h_{0}(W,1,X)-h_{0}(W,0,X)\mid X=x]. (3) Equation 3 identifies the effect conditional on X X alone by averaging over the proxies. Early approaches to recovering this bridge function focused on parametric proximal g-computation. Under linear specifications, proximal g-computation reduces to a two-stage estimation procedure closely related to instrumental variable methods. While computationally efficient, proximal two-stage least squares ( P2SLS , Tchetgen Tchetgen et al., 2020 ) relies heavily on strict parametric assumptions. To capture more complex confounding mechanisms, recent two-stage methods have replaced linear regressions with highly flexible nonparametric approximators, such as kernel proxy variable ( KPV , Mastouri et al., 2021 ) and deep feature proxy variable ( Xu et al., 2021 ) . An alternative is to estimate the outcome bridge function by directly enforcing the conditional moment restriction equivalent to Equation 2 . Proxy maximum moment restriction ( PMMR , Mastouri et al., 2021 ) leverages a reproducing kernel Hilbert space, while neural maximum moment restriction ( NMMR , Kompa et al., 2022 ) extends this approach by using neural networks. A separate strand of methods are doubly-robust meta-learners for heterogeneous treatment effect estimation, e.g. P-learner from Sverdrup and Cui (2023) and the Forster-Warmuth learner of ( Yang et al., 2023 ) . They estimate an outcome bridge and a treatment bridge functions, then constructs a pseudo-outcome from them. These outcomes are used to fit a standard conditional mean regression mapping the domain of covariates X X to treatment effect. While these modern approaches are highly adaptive, they introduce their own practical hurdles. They demand complex, dataset-specific hyperparameter tuning and extensive model retraining from scratch for every new causal task. The kernel methods also require the computation of kernel matrices, which can impose computational and memory burden in large sample sizes. This motivates the search for an amortized alternative capable of directly estimating Q ⁡ ( x ) Q(x) from observational context.

sections.heading: 3 ProximalFM
sections.text: We propose ProximalFM , a PFN for proximal causal inference. Pre-trained on synthetic proximal models, ProximalFM predicts a posterior distribution over Q ⁡ ( x ) Q(x) from an observational context and query covariates x x . Unlike existing approaches, it does this without explicitly solving an ill-posed inverse problem as an intermediate step. Instead, it directly outputs a CATE posterior from a single forward pass of a neural network.

sections.heading: Enforcing proximal assumptions.
sections.text: By construction, every SCM drawn from Π \Pi is designed to satisfy the identification conditions of Section 2.1 (see Section B.3 for empirical diagnostics): • Structural constraints ( 1 & 2 ). By construction in ( 4 ), mutual independence of the exogenous noises ϵ ( . ) \epsilon_{(.)} and the specified mechanism inputs encode the required exclusions. The corresponding conditional independencies follow immediately for every sampled SCM. • Positivity ( 3 ). Guaranteed by clamping treatment assignment probabilities to [ δ , 1 − δ ] [\delta,1-\delta] with δ > 0 \delta>0 before sampling A A . • Completeness ( 4 ). Unlike structural graph constraints, completeness is a more subtle, distribution-level condition: it is untestable in observational data and cannot be strictly guaranteed by construction for arbitrary non-linear mechanisms ( Tchetgen Tchetgen et al., 2020 ) . The prior therefore relies on a heuristic requiring the dimensions of W W and Z Z to be greater than the one of U U . Their cardinalities also dominate the one of U U (see Section B.2.4 ).

sections.heading: Encoding the proximal setting.
sections.text: The backbone of ProximalFM follows the TabICLv2 architecture ( Qu et al., 2026 ) ; we defer architectural details to Section C.1 . Our modifications concern the input processing which must carry the causal role of each column as the roles of ( X , Z , W ) (X,Z,W) are not identifiable from their position or values. ProximalFM differs from regular tabular models such as TabICLv2 in two respects. First, its target is not observed in the context: the ITE is never observed, only the factual outcome Y = Y ⁡ ( A ) Y=Y(A) is. These observations only provide evidence about the underlying SCM and its CATE function Q ⁡ ( x ) Q(x) . Second, ProximalFM targets the posterior distribution over the CATE, p ⁡ ( Q ⁡ ( x ⋆ ) ∣ 𝒟 N ) p\bigl(Q(x^{\star})\mid\mathcal{D}_{N}\bigr) , rather than a distribution over an individual-level label such as the ITE. Each query is represented by x ⋆ x^{\star} only: including its proxy values ( w ⋆ , z ⋆ ) (w^{\star},z^{\star}) would condition the prediction on the proxies and change the target away from the CATE Q ⁡ ( x ⋆ ) Q(x^{\star}) . We add structural role embeddings , a learnable token per feature group ( X X , Z Z , W W ), added to its column embeddings. A treatment-aware target encoder is also implemented. It consists of two linear projections of the outcome selected by the treatment indicator A A , so that outcomes observed under treatment and control are embedded separately ( Figure 3 ).

sections.heading: Methods evaluated.
sections.text: We compare ProximalFM against three families of methods. First, proximal estimators recover causal effects through bridge functions or conditional moment restrictions. These are the only baselines encoding the proximal identification assumptions. Second, we evaluate existing causal foundation models that assume no unmeasured confounding. Third, conventional S-, T-, and X-meta-learners provide other non-proximal backdoor baselines ( Künzel et al., 2019 ) . The backdoor methods are evaluated by either fitting X X alone or fitting ( X , W , Z ) (X,W,Z) followed by marginalizing the proxy-conditional contrast over the proxies. Both variants return a function of x x , but neither is generally identified as Q ⁡ ( x ) Q(x) under the proximal assumptions. Section D.1 lists all methods and refers to their configuration and implementation details.

sections.heading: Datasets.
sections.text: Section D.2 details our semi-synthetic datasets generation. The covariates X X and unobserved U U are features from real-world data. The proxies W W and Z Z are then generated from ( U , X ) (U,X) . Similarly, the treatment assignment A A and outcomes Y ⁡ ( 1 ) , Y ⁡ ( 0 ) Y(1),Y(0) are generated from ( U , X ) (U,X) . Note that we don’t use Z Z and W W as direct inputs when generating the treatment and outcomes. This semi-synthetic approach grounds the simulation on real-world features, while having control over dataset properties such as confounding strength of U U and proxy informativeness of ( W , Z ) (W,Z) about U U . We consider a factorial design crossing linear versus nonlinear mechanisms, low versus high latent-confounding strength, and low versus high proxy informativeness, yielding eight configurations. For each of the eight settings, we evaluate 12 datasets with three independent replicates each, giving a total of 288 evaluation instances. We set d X = d U = d W = d Z = 5 d_{X}=d_{U}=d_{W}=d_{Z}=5 .

sections.heading: ProximalFM is competitive across settings.
sections.text: Figure 4 summarizes the performance of selected methods, with detailed results available in Tables D.7 – D.10 . Across all eight settings, ProximalFM is competitive, with its clearest advantage at larger context sizes under high confounding and low proxy reliability. Among the proximal methods, P-learner (TabICL) is also consistently competitive, but typically requires larger context sizes to obtain good performance. KPV and PMMR generally underperform, possibly because of the use of kernel-based bridge functions in this moderate dimension regime ( d X = d U = d W = d Z = 5 d_{X}=d_{U}=d_{W}=d_{Z}=5 ). Flexible backdoor methods such as S-learner (TabICL) and CausalPFN perform surprisingly well when combined with simple proxy marginalization. Their performance deteriorates, however, when strong confounding is combined with low proxy information. Figure 4: Median CATE nPEHE across benchmark episodes versus context size. Rows show linear and nonlinear mechanisms; columns vary latent confounding and proxy reliability. The dotted line marks the constant-ATE baseline ( nPEHE = 1 \mathrm{nPEHE}=1 ); lower is better.

sections.heading: ProximalFM plateaus beyond its training range.
sections.text: We next consider the nonlinear regime with high latent confounding and low proxy reliability ( Figure D.2 , Table D.11 ). This is a particularly relevant proximal setting: the confounding cannot be ignored, the proxy signal is weak and thus conditioning on proxies is insufficient. As the context grows beyond n ctx = 2 048 n_{\mathrm{ctx}}=2\,048 , the P-learner (TabICL) continues to improve and becomes the strongest method, whereas ProximalFM improves little further and remains close to the constant-ATE baseline. A plausible explanation is a mismatch between evaluation and pre-training context sizes: ProximalFM was trained on contexts of at most 2 048 2\,048 observations. To assess this, we continue training the model for limited time on episodes with contexts of up to 5 000 5\,000 observations ( Section C.3.1 , ProximalFM-FT ). The adapted model shows small improvements at large context sizes, consistent with limited large-context training support contributing to the observed plateau.

sections.heading: ProximalFM is fast and requires no task-specific tuning.
sections.text: ProximalFM lies on a favourable accuracy–runtime frontier ( Figure 5 ). It achieves among the strongest CATE ranks while requiring little end-to-end runtime compared to several competing proximal methods. Moving inference from CPU to MPS further reduces its runtime without changing its predictions. ProximalFM does not require hyperparameter selection, simplifying deployment and making its reported runtime unaffected by the choice of a selection grid. Figure 5: Accuracy and speed at context size n = 2 048 n=2\,048 , shown separately for linear and nonlinear mechanisms. Points show median runtime per episode against median paired CATE nPEHE rank (IQR whiskers). Filled and hollow points respectively include and exclude hyperparameter selection. The orange segment compares ProximalFM on CPU and MPS. More details in Section D.3.1 .

sections.heading: The posterior is overconfident on semi-synthetic data.
sections.text: Figure D.3 compares nominal and empirical credible-interval coverage. On datasets sampled from the pre-training prior, coverage is close to nominal across all context sizes, and posterior uncertainty contracts steadily as the context grows. On the other hand, on the semi-synthetic datasets, the posterior is increasingly overconfident as the context size grows. This undercoverage under distribution shift is consistent with the out-of-distribution experiments from Balazadeh Meresht et al. (2026) . Notably, the posterior standard deviation continues to decrease beyond the maximum pre-training context size.

sections.heading: Proxy informativeness matters.
sections.text: The good performance of TabICL and CausalPFN in the semi-synthetic benchmark raises the question of whether flexible backdoor methods can substitute for proximal estimation. We investigate this in a setting with linear outcome and Gaussian proxy mechanisms, where we control the information that ( W , Z ) (W,Z) carries about U U ( Section D.4 ). At n ctx = 2 048 n_{\mathrm{ctx}}=2\,048 , ProximalFM outperforms proxy-marginalized CausalPFN throughout the sweep and proxy-adjusted linear regression (OLS) in most settings, although OLS catches up when proxies nearly reveal U U . Well specified proximal 2SLS ( Tchetgen Tchetgen et al., 2020 ) provides a reference for what matching the estimator to this mechanism can achieve.

sections.heading: Towards a real physical evaluation.
sections.text: We compare ATE estimations on Causal Chambers, a physical system with a known causal graph ( Gamella et al., 2025 ) ( Appendix E ). Backdoor meta-learners outperform proximal learners, including ProximalFM . We interpret this cautiously: ProximalFM is designed for CATE, this benchmark has only twelve configurations of one one-dimensional system and moderate sample size ( 1 000 1\,000 observations each).

sections.heading: 5 Conclusion
sections.text: We introduced ProximalFM , an amortized estimator for CATE under the proximal learning assumptions. Existing causal foundation models address settings such as backdoor, instrumental-variable, and frontdoor identification, but are not designed to exploit proxies for proximal identification. Rather than solving an ill-posed bridge equation separately for each new dataset, ProximalFM learns from synthetic episodes to estimate CATE from observational data, with regularization implied by the prior. Its CATE posterior also provides uncertainty estimates, though credible intervals can be overconfident beyond the training prior. Together with models for other identification settings, it gives practitioners a fast way to compare estimates under different plausible identifying assumptions.

sections.heading: B.1 Step-by-step procedure
sections.text: We generate each synthetic dataset from an independently sampled structural causal model (SCM) compatible with the proximal DAG. The full routine is sketched in Figure B.1 and specified in Algorithm 1 ; this section walks through it and fixes notation used across Appendix B . Throughout, a dataset consists of T T units (the sequence length) and the target estimand is the conditional average treatment effect Q ⁡ ( x ) = 𝔼 ⁡ [ Y ⁡ ( 1 ) − Y ⁡ ( 0 ) ∣ X = x ] Q(x)=\mathbb{E}[Y(1)-Y(0)\mid X=x] . Because Q ⁡ ( x ) Q(x) marginalises over all unit-level heterogeneity beyond X X , we approximate the conditional expected potential outcomes (CEPOs) μ a ​ ( x ) = 𝔼 ⁡ [ Y ⁡ ( a ) ∣ X = x ] \mu_{a}(x)=\mathbb{E}[Y(a)\mid X=x] by Monte Carlo integration: every unit is replicated K K times, sharing its covariate value x x while drawing fresh exogenous noise—and therefore fresh latent-confounder and proxy realizations—and the potential outcomes are averaged over the K K replicates.

sections.text: We first sample the latent and observed dimensionalities, drawing the confounder dimension d U d_{U} from a law skewed toward small values and then the proxy dimensions d W , d Z d_{W},d_{Z} conditionally on d U d_{U} so as to respect the completeness heuristic d W , d Z ≥ d U d_{W},d_{Z}\geq d_{U} , with the covariate dimension d X d_{X} drawn independently and uniformly; the sampling laws and the resulting induced marginals are described below in Section B.2.2 . We then instantiate the causal mechanisms f X , f U , f W , f Z , f A , f Y f_{X},f_{U},f_{W},f_{Z},f_{A},f_{Y} as independently initialised random multilayer perceptrons in the style of TabICL ( Qu et al., 2025 ) , together with an auxiliary confounding-duplication network f aug f_{\mathrm{aug}} (described below), and sample the per-dataset hyperparameters (network depth, width, activations, noise scales; see Section B.2.1 ). Mechanisms, dimensions and hyperparameters are held fixed across all T T units and their K K replicates, so the entire dataset is drawn from the same SCM.

sections.heading: B.2.2 Dimensions & dimension heuristic
sections.text: The block dimensions are sampled according to the completeness heuristic introduced in Section B.1 . The confounder dimension is drawn from a triangular (linearly decreasing) law on { 1 , … , d U max } \{1,\dots,d_{U}^{\max}\} , Pr [ d U = d ] ∝ ( d U max + 1 − d ) , \Pr[d_{U}=d]\;\propto\;(d_{U}^{\max}+1-d), (22) which skews d U d_{U} toward small values. Conditional on d U d_{U} , the two proxy dimensions are sampled uniformly subject to d W , d Z ≥ d U d_{W},d_{Z}\geq d_{U} , while the covariate dimension d X d_{X} is sampled independently and uniformly: d W ∼ Unif ⁡ { d U , … , d W max } , d Z ∼ Unif ⁡ { d U , … , d Z max } , d X ∼ Unif ⁡ { d X min , … , d X max } . d_{W}\sim\mathrm{Unif}\{d_{U},\dots,d_{W}^{\max}\},\quad d_{Z}\sim\mathrm{Unif}\{d_{U},\dots,d_{Z}^{\max}\},\quad d_{X}\sim\mathrm{Unif}\{d_{X}^{\min},\dots,d_{X}^{\max}\}. (23) This conditional-uniform sampling has a convenient consequence in the common-bound configuration used here, where d U d_{U} , d W d_{W} , and d Z d_{Z} all range from 1 1 to a shared maximum m m . When d U d_{U} follows the triangular law, the weight ( m + 1 − d ) (m+1-d) placed on d U = d d_{U}=d exactly cancels the normaliser 1 / ( m − d + 1 ) 1/(m-d+1) of the conditional uniform, so the induced marginal of each proxy dimension is the linear ramp Pr [ d W = w ] = w ∑ j = 1 m j = 2 ​ w m ⁡ ( m + 1 ) , w ∈ { 1 , … , m } , \Pr[d_{W}=w]\;=\;\frac{w}{\sum_{j=1}^{m}j}\;=\;\frac{2w}{m(m+1)},\qquad w\in\{1,\dots,m\}, (24) and likewise for d Z d_{Z} . The triangular choice for d U d_{U} is what buys this. Had d U d_{U} been uniform, the same conditional sampling would induce a harmonic proxy marginal, Pr [ d W = w ] = ( H m − H m − w ) / m \Pr[d_{W}=w]=(H_{m}-H_{m-w})/m with H n H_{n} the n n -th harmonic number, which piles proxy mass against the ceiling m m : the value w = m w=m is reachable from every d U d_{U} , whereas small w w requires a small d U d_{U} , so probability accumulates at the top (for m = 10 m=10 , Pr [ d W = 10 ] = 0.29 \Pr[d_{W}=10]=0.29 ). The triangular law flattens this to the linear ramp of ( 24 ) ( Pr [ d W = 10 ] = 0.18 \Pr[d_{W}=10]=0.18 ), and lowers the mean confounder and proxy dimensions from 5.5 5.5 and 7.75 7.75 to 4.0 4.0 and 7.0 7.0 respectively. Figure B.2 shows the delivered marginals of both schemes against these analytic laws. sections.heading: B.2.3 MLP generation, noise & edge sampling
sections.text: TabICL builds a single random MLP that turns a block of root “causes” into one feature table, reading its columns from the pooled activations of the MLP’s intermediate layers. We reuse that construction unchanged as the mechanism for each individual node – the layer stack, the random activation library, the block-sparse or dropout-masked Gaussian initialisation, and the pooled-output selection, all sampled once per dataset ( Table B.3 ); we refer to TabICL for these details ( Qu et al., 2025 ) . In ProximalFM , the innovative step is that a proximal dataset is not one block but a chain of them, f X , f U , f W , f Z , f A , f Y f_{X},f_{U},f_{W},f_{Z},f_{A},f_{Y} along a proximal learning DAG. Wiring one block into the next raises two questions a single-MLP generator never faces: • How should a parent block enter the child’s mechanism? • How should we inject fresh per-node randomness while keeping it proportional to the signal?

sections.heading: Parents and noise.
sections.text: The root mechanism has no parents and maps a sampled noise input block straight to the covariates, X = f X ​ ( ε X ) X=f_{X}(\varepsilon_{X}) . Every downstream mechanism instead concatenates its standardised parent blocks with a fresh input block of its own, e.g. U = f U ​ ( X ~ U , ε U ) U=f_{U}(\tilde{X}_{U},\varepsilon_{U}) as in ( 21 ). These per-node blocks ε ( ⋅ ) \varepsilon_{(\cdot)} play the role of exogenous noise: we draw them from the same sampler TabICL uses for its root causes – each column independently normal, uniform, multinomial, or clamped Zipf under per-dataset mixing weights – and size each to a per-dataset share of its mechanism’s signal width ( Table B.3 ), so the noise-to-signal ratio stays controlled rather than shrinking as the parent blocks grow. The MLP’s own within-layer Gaussian perturbation is left small ( noise_std = 10 − 3 \texttt{noise\_std}=10^{-3} ), so in practice the input blocks carry essentially all of a node’s exogenous randomness. Postprocessing Corrupt ⁡ ( ⋅ ) \mathrm{Corrupt}(\cdot) ( Section B.2.4 ) then reshapes each block before it is consumed.

sections.heading: Edge sampling.
sections.text: At the MLP level, the parent blocks above are passed through dataset-specific column masks. For each mechanism that depends on X X , we draw a keep probability from Unif ⁡ [ 0 , 1 ] \mathrm{Unif}[0,1] and retain the columns of X ~ \tilde{X} independently according to that probability. The same procedure is applied to the W → Y W\to Y and Z → A Z\to A links, producing the masked proxy inputs W ~ Y \tilde{W}_{Y} and Z ~ A \tilde{Z}_{A} . Thus edge sampling can only remove potential parents from the fixed proximal DAG: the completeness links Z ← U → W Z\leftarrow U\rightarrow W remain intact, and no new dependencies are introduced. The resulting subgraphs therefore retain the dimensionality heuristic and the structural proximal restrictions. The separate control of how strongly U U enters f A f_{A} and f Y f_{Y} is described next.

sections.heading: Confounding control.
sections.text: In a random MLP the confounder’s influence on A A and Y Y would be pinned by U U ’s share of each mechanism’s input width, hence by d U d_{U} ; to decouple confounding strength from d U d_{U} we target a share s A , s Y ∼ Beta ⁡ ( 1.2 , 2.8 ) s_{A},s_{Y}\sim\mathrm{Beta}(1.2,2.8) of the inputs to f A , f Y f_{A},f_{Y} to be U U -derived and translate it into a column count k k . When k k does not exceed d U d_{U} the mechanism sees a k k -column subsample of U U ; when it does, it sees all of U U plus ( k − d U ) (k-d_{U}) extra columns drawn from a shared nonlinear re-encoding U aug = f aug ​ ( U ~ ) U^{\mathrm{aug}}=f_{\mathrm{aug}}(\tilde{U}) , itself a random MLP, giving the confounding-controlled inputs U [ A ] , U [ Y ] U^{[A]},U^{[Y]} . Since f aug f_{\mathrm{aug}} is a deterministic function of U U , these extra columns carry no information beyond U U – they only let the prior push confounding above what d U d_{U} alone would permit, without altering the DAG or the completeness edges. Numerically , we keep d W , d Z ≥ d U d_{W},d_{Z}\geq d_{U} . sections.heading: B.2.5 Treatment assignment
sections.text: The treatment mechanism f A f_{A} maps the confounding-controlled confounder input U [ A ] U^{[A]} , the covariate subset X ~ A \tilde{X}_{A} , the direct proxy subset Z ~ A \tilde{Z}_{A} and fresh noise ε A \varepsilon_{A} to a single scalar logit per row, ℓ = f A ​ ( U [ A ] , X ~ A , Z ~ A , ε A ) ∈ ℝ T ​ K , \ell\;=\;f_{A}\big(U^{[A]},\,\tilde{X}_{A},\,\tilde{Z}_{A},\,\varepsilon_{A}\big)\;\in\;\mathbb{R}^{TK}, (25) with W W excluded from the inputs so that the proxy exclusion restriction of Assumption 2 holds by construction (Equation 21 ). The treatment A A is binary; the steps below turn ℓ \ell into a propensity score π = Pr [ A = 1 ∣ ⋅ ] \pi=\Pr[A=1\mid\cdot] and draw A A .

sections.heading: Logit normalisation.
sections.text: A random MLP fixes neither the location nor the spread of its output, both of which drift with depth, width and input scale; left raw, the induced treatment prevalence and the amount of overlap would be an uncontrolled by-product of the sampled architecture. We therefore standardise the logits across the T ⋅ K T\cdot K rows of the dataset to zero mean and unit variance, ℓ ~ = ℓ − ℓ ¯ sd ⁡ ( ℓ ) + 10 − 8 , \tilde{\ell}\;=\;\frac{\ell-\bar{\ell}}{\operatorname{sd}(\ell)+10^{-8}}, (26) so that the assignment distribution is decoupled from the accidental scale of f A f_{A} and every dataset starts from a common footing before the overlap knobs act.

sections.heading: Shift and scale.
sections.text: Two per-dataset propensity knobs then set the assignment regime through an affine map of the standardised logits, ℓ ′ = s ​ ℓ ~ + b , b ∼ Unif ⁡ ( − 2.5 , 2.5 ) , s ∼ log-scaled truncated normal , \ell^{\prime}\;=\;s\,\tilde{\ell}+b,\qquad b\sim\mathrm{Unif}(-2.5,\,2.5),\quad s\sim\text{log-scaled truncated normal}, (27) both drawn once per dataset (see Table B.3 ). The shift b b moves the marginal treatment prevalence away from the balanced split – negative b b makes treatment rare, positive b b makes it common – while the scale s s controls how sharply assignment depends on the covariates and confounder: small s s flattens the logits toward a coin flip (strong overlap, weak confounding channelled through A A ), whereas large s s sharpens them toward near-deterministic assignment (weaker overlap).

sections.heading: B.2.6 Potential outcomes & heterogeneity remix
sections.text: The outcome mechanism f Y f_{Y} emits both potential outcomes from a single forward pass, returning the pair ( Y 0 raw , Y 1 raw ) \big(Y_{0}^{\mathrm{raw}},Y_{1}^{\mathrm{raw}}\big) from a common input and exogenous draw ε Y \varepsilon_{Y} ; the two arms differ only in their read-out, so the raw effect τ raw = Y 1 raw − Y 0 raw \tau^{\mathrm{raw}}=Y_{1}^{\mathrm{raw}}-Y_{0}^{\mathrm{raw}} stays coupled through the shared latent state. sections.heading: C.1 Architecture
sections.text: ProximalFM encodes a dataset in the three sequential stages of TabICLv2 ( Qu et al., 2026 ) , which we use unchanged. A column embedder maps each scalar cell to an embedding through a shared inducing-point set transformer applied along the unit axis, so that a cell is represented relative to the empirical distribution of its own column. A row interactor then treats the embedded cells of a unit as a sequence of tokens along the column axis, applies a transformer with rotary positional encoding, and concatenates the outputs of n cls n_{\mathrm{cls}} prepended learnable CLS tokens into a single vector per unit. Finally, an in-context learner runs a transformer over the sequence of unit vectors in which query units attend to context units but not to one another; no positional encoding is applied along the unit axis, so the model is equivariant to the ordering of the dataset. All blocks are pre-norm and use the query-aware scalable softmax of Qu et al. (2026) . Our only removals are the classification-specific components, which a continuous causal estimand does not use; the remaining departures are described below.

sections.heading: A target that is never observed.
sections.text: Every departure below follows from one change of task. In tabular in-context learning the query is a context row with a missing label: the model predicts y ⋆ y^{\star} , the same variable it has just seen realized in the context, and the query differs from a context unit only in that one entry is withheld. ProximalFM predicts Q ⁡ ( x ⋆ ) = 𝔼 ⁡ [ Y ⁡ ( 1 ) − Y ⁡ ( 0 ) ∣ X = x ⋆ ] Q(x^{\star})=\mathbb{E}[Y(1)-Y(0)\mid X=x^{\star}] , which is realized for no unit in the table. The observed columns are evidence about the mechanism that generates it, and supervision comes from the prior’s oracle targets rather than from held-out labels. Two context columns consequently have no query counterpart. The outcome y y is context-only in TabICL as well, but there it is withheld because it is the answer; here it is withheld because a query unit is a covariate profile, not a realized unit, and the same holds for the treatment a a : the estimand averages over both arms, so no value of a a can sensibly be attached to the query vector x ⋆ x^{\star} . The proxies are a different case. A query unit can have a w ⋆ w^{\star} and a z ⋆ z^{\star} , and the prior generates them, so withholding them is a design choice rather than a structural necessity: conditioning on them would target 𝔼 [ Y ( 1 ) − Y ( 0 ) ∣ X , W , Z ] \mathbb{E}[Y(1)-Y(0)\mid X,W,Z] instead. We follow the proximal literature in conditioning on the baseline covariates alone ( Section 2.2 ) and marginalizing over the proxies. At inference the model therefore sees the context table in full and a query reduced to x ⋆ x^{\star} alone. The modifications below adapt the backbone to exactly this interface.

sections.heading: Structural role embeddings.
sections.text: The backbone from TabICL consumes a single undifferentiated feature matrix, whereas proximal identification treats the three observed blocks asymmetrically: the roles of Z Z , W W and X X are necessary to be known in order to infer the causal estimand of interest. Nothing in the values themselves reveals that role. Column order alone cannot supply it either: the block sizes ( d X , d Z , d W ) (d_{X},d_{Z},d_{W}) are resampled for every dataset, so no fixed column index marks where one block ends and the next begins, and the model would have to infer the two boundaries from the data before it could use them. We therefore tag the role explicitly. Writing lin ⁡ ( ⋅ ) \mathrm{lin}(\cdot) for the shared cell projection into ℝ E \mathbb{R}^{E} , a cell v v of block g ∈ { X , Z , W } g\in\{X,Z,W\} enters the column embedder as lin ⁡ ( v ) + r g , r X , r Z , r W ∈ ℝ E ​ learnable , \mathrm{lin}(v)+r_{g},\qquad r_{X},\,r_{Z},\,r_{W}\in\mathbb{R}^{E}\text{ learnable}, (31) after which the three blocks are concatenated along the column axis into a single sequence of d X + d Z + d W d_{X}+d_{Z}+d_{W} columns. Role identity is thus carried by the embedding rather than by position. The treatment A A is not passed as a column at all: it enters only through the target encoder described next.

sections.heading: Treatment-aware target encoder.
sections.text: The remaining two observed variables, y y and a a , are not handled the way X X , Z Z and W W are. They are present for context units and absent for queries, so instead of being concatenated to the input row as columns, they are added to the tokens of context units. This also settles how a a is encoded: it qualifies y y rather than standing beside it, since an outcome means one thing under treatment and another under control. We therefore hold two projections and select between them with the observed treatment indicator, enc ⁡ ( y i , a i ) = ( 1 − a i ) ​ lin y 0 ​ ( y i ) + a i ​ lin y 1 ​ ( y i ) , lin y 0 , lin y 1 : ℝ → ℝ E . \mathrm{enc}(y_{i},a_{i})=(1-a_{i})\,\mathrm{lin}_{y_{0}}(y_{i})+a_{i}\,\mathrm{lin}_{y_{1}}(y_{i}),\qquad\mathrm{lin}_{y_{0}},\,\mathrm{lin}_{y_{1}}:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}^{E}. (32) Outcome and arm are thus encoded jointly, and the treated and control response surfaces may occupy different directions in embedding space from the first layer onwards. The encoder is applied at two points, the column embedder and the in-context learner, with untied parameters.

sections.heading: Standardization and query-row proxy masking.
sections.text: Each of X X , Z Z , W W and y y is standardized column-wise using the empirical mean and standard deviation of the context units only, so that no query information reaches the model through the scale and predictions are invariant to affine rescaling of the inputs. A query unit is then presented without its proxies. The Z Z and W W positions of query rows are filled with a fixed value of 0 0 and then masked out of the attention in the row interactor, so those tokens do not merely carry a neutral value but are invisible to the query representation altogether. The same protocol applies during training and at inference time.

sections.heading: Output head.
sections.text: For each query unit the in-context learner emits B B logits, passed through a softmax to give the predictive distribution q θ [ ⋅ ∣ x ⋆ , 𝒟 N ] q_{\theta}[\,\cdot\mid x^{\star},\mathcal{D}_{N}] over a fixed grid of B B equal-width bins spanning [ v min , v max ] [v_{\min},v_{\max}] , expressed in units of the context standard deviation of y y . Discretizing the predictive distribution in this way is standard practice for PFNs ( Hollmann et al., 2023 ) and is what allows a single forward pass to return a full distribution without committing to a parametric family; amortized causal models adopt it as well ( Balazadeh Meresht et al., 2026 ) . A single head is placed directly over the CATE rather than one head per arm. Although Q ⁡ ( x ) = μ 1 ​ ( x ) − μ 0 ​ ( x ) Q(x)=\mu_{1}(x)-\mu_{0}(x) , the two CEPOs are functionals of the same unknown SCM and are therefore generally dependent under its posterior given 𝒟 N \mathcal{D}_{N} . Their marginal posterior distributions alone do not determine the posterior of their difference: convolving them would implicitly impose posterior independence and omit their covariance, which can misstate the CATE uncertainty. Directly learning the distribution of Q ⁡ ( x ) Q(x) avoids this unsupported joint-posterior assumption. Two properties of the discretization matter for what follows. First, we read the bin probabilities as a piecewise-uniform density rather than as point masses at the bin centers. This is what makes the noise convolution of ( 34 ) exact, and it puts a floor of w / 12 w/\sqrt{12} — the standard deviation of a single bin, of width w = ( v max − v min ) / B w=(v_{\max}-v_{\min})/B — on any posterior standard deviation the head can report. Second, the grid is a hard support constraint: a target outside [ v min , v max ] [v_{\min},v_{\max}] cannot be represented at all, so the bounds must be wide enough to cover the CATE distribution the prior produces. Chosen v max v_{\max} , v min v_{\min} and B B are reported in Table C.1 .

sections.heading: C.2 The noise-aware histogram loss
sections.text: This section gives the closed form of the training objective of Section 3.2 , together with the motivation for scoring a noise-convolved predictive distribution rather than fitting the Monte Carlo targets directly.

sections.heading: Notation and standardization.
sections.text: All quantities below live on the context-standardized scale. For a dataset with N N context rows, let m N m_{N} and s N s_{N} denote the empirical mean and standard deviation of the observed outcomes { y i } i = 1 N \{y_{i}\}_{i=1}^{N} . Outcomes are standardized as ( y − m N ) / s N (y-m_{N})/s_{N} , so the CATE target and its Monte Carlo variance enter as t i ≔ Q ^ K ​ ( x i ) s N , ς i 2 ≔ S i 2 s N 2 , t_{i}\coloneqq\frac{\hat{Q}_{K}(x_{i})}{s_{N}},\qquad\varsigma_{i}^{2}\coloneqq\frac{S_{i}^{2}}{s_{N}^{2}}, (33) the location shift m N m_{N} cancelling in the difference μ ^ 1 − μ ^ 0 \hat{\mu}_{1}-\hat{\mu}_{0} . Because m N m_{N} and s N s_{N} are computed on context rows only, no query information leaks into the scale. The head emits B B logits over a fixed uniform grid e 1 < e 2 < ⋯ < e B + 1 e_{1}<e_{2}<\dots<e_{B+1} spanning [ v min , v max ] [v_{\min},v_{\max}] with bin width w = ( v max − v min ) / B w=(v_{\max}-v_{\min})/B , and q θ [ b ∣ x i , 𝒟 N ] q_{\theta}[b\mid x_{i},\mathcal{D}_{N}] denotes the predicted probability of bin b = [ e b , e b + 1 ) b=[e_{b},e_{b+1}) . We write Φ \Phi for the standard normal CDF. The quantity σ 2 \sigma^{2} denotes the variance of an auxiliary Gaussian smoothing kernel , expressed on this standardized scale; it is distinct from the row-specific Monte Carlo variance ς i 2 \varsigma_{i}^{2} and is annealed during training according to the schedule described in Section C.3 .

sections.heading: Closed form.
sections.text: Whereas q θ q_{\theta} is the model’s predictive distribution over the estimand Q ⁡ ( x i ) Q(x_{i}) , the quantity actually observed during training is the noisy measurement t i t_{i} ; q ~ θ \tilde{q}_{\theta} is the predictive density that q θ q_{\theta} induces over that measurement. Write the per-row variance as κ i 2 ≔ ς i 2 + σ 2 \kappa_{i}^{2}\coloneqq\varsigma_{i}^{2}+\sigma^{2} , combining the known target noise with the annealed smoothing scale (also known). Conditioning on which bin contains the estimand, the law of total probability gives q ~ θ ​ ( t ∣ x i , 𝒟 N ) \displaystyle\tilde{q}_{\theta}\bigl(t\mid x_{i},\mathcal{D}_{N}\bigr) = ∑ b = 1 B ℙ ⁡ ( Q ∈ [ e b , e b + 1 ) ∣ x i , 𝒟 N ) ⋅ p ⁡ ( t ∣ Q ∈ [ e b , e b + 1 ) ) \displaystyle=\sum_{b=1}^{B}\vphantom{\Bigl[}\mathbb{P}\bigl(Q\in[e_{b},e_{b+1})\mid x_{i},\mathcal{D}_{N}\bigr)\;\cdot\;\vphantom{\Bigl[}p\bigl(t\mid Q\in[e_{b},e_{b+1})\bigr) = ∑ b = 1 B q θ [ b ∣ x i , 𝒟 N ] 1 w [ Φ ( e b + 1 − t κ i ) − Φ ( e b − t κ i ) ] . \displaystyle=\sum_{b=1}^{B}q_{\theta}[b\mid x_{i},\mathcal{D}_{N}]\;\frac{1}{w}\left[\Phi\!\left(\frac{e_{b+1}-t}{\kappa_{i}}\right)-\Phi\!\left(\frac{e_{b}-t}{\kappa_{i}}\right)\right]. (34) The first factor is read straight off the head. The second follows from the piecewise-uniform continuous reading of the histogram: given that Q Q lies in bin b b , the head places it uniformly within that bin, so p ⁡ ( t ∣ Q ∈ [ e b , e b + 1 ) ) = ∫ e b e b + 1 1 w ​ 𝒩 ​ ( t , u , κ i 2 ) ​ ⁡ 𝑑 u = 1 w ​ [ Φ ⁡ ( e b + 1 − t κ i ) − Φ ⁡ ( e b − t κ i ) ] , p\bigl(t\mid Q\in[e_{b},e_{b+1})\bigr)=\int_{e_{b}}^{e_{b+1}}\frac{1}{w}\,\mathcal{N}\bigl(t;\,u,\,\kappa_{i}^{2}\bigr)\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}u=\frac{1}{w}\left[\Phi\!\left(\frac{e_{b+1}-t}{\kappa_{i}}\right)-\Phi\!\left(\frac{e_{b}-t}{\kappa_{i}}\right)\right], (35) where the integral runs over the mean of the Gaussian. The training objective is the negative log-likelihood of the observed target under ( 34 ), evaluated at t = t i t=t_{i} : ℒ noise ​ _ ​ aware = − 1 n q ∑ i = 1 n q log ( ∑ b = 1 B q θ [ b ∣ x i , 𝒟 N ] 1 w [ Φ ( e b + 1 − t i κ i ) − Φ ( e b − t i κ i ) ] ) . \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{noise\_aware}}=-\frac{1}{n_{q}}\sum_{i=1}^{n_{q}}\log\left(\sum_{b=1}^{B}q_{\theta}[b\mid x_{i},\mathcal{D}_{N}]\;\frac{1}{w}\left[\Phi\!\left(\frac{e_{b+1}-t_{i}}{\kappa_{i}}\right)-\Phi\!\left(\frac{e_{b}-t_{i}}{\kappa_{i}}\right)\right]\right). (36)

sections.heading: Why convolve the model rather than fit the target.
sections.text: Consider the population risk of ( 36 ) at fixed context. The target is distributed as t ∼ p ( ⋅ ∣ 𝒟 N ) ∗ 𝒩 ( 0 , ς 2 ) t\sim p(\,\cdot\mid\mathcal{D}_{N})\ast\mathcal{N}(0,\varsigma^{2}) , the posterior over the estimand blurred by Monte Carlo error. A negative log-likelihood is minimized when the scored density matches the density of the data, i.e. when q θ ∗ 𝒩 ( 0 , ς 2 + σ 2 ) = p ( ⋅ ∣ 𝒟 N ) ∗ 𝒩 ( 0 , ς 2 ) ⟺ q θ ∗ 𝒩 ( 0 , σ 2 ) = p ( ⋅ ∣ 𝒟 N ) . q_{\theta}\ast\mathcal{N}(0,\varsigma^{2}+\sigma^{2})=p(\,\cdot\mid\mathcal{D}_{N})\ast\mathcal{N}(0,\varsigma^{2})\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad q_{\theta}\ast\mathcal{N}(0,\sigma^{2})=p(\,\cdot\mid\mathcal{D}_{N}). (37) The Monte Carlo variance cancels on both sides: the correction is exact for any value of σ \sigma , and the recovered q θ q_{\theta} converges to the posterior as σ \sigma is annealed. Fitting the same head directly to t i t_{i} instead—the noise-unaware objective—has population optimum q θ = p ( ⋅ ∣ 𝒟 N ) ∗ 𝒩 ( 0 , ς 2 + σ 2 ) q_{\theta}=p(\,\cdot\mid\mathcal{D}_{N})\ast\mathcal{N}(0,\varsigma^{2}+\sigma^{2}) , over-dispersed by exactly the target noise. The distortion is not a constant offset that could be calibrated away post hoc: ς i 2 = Var ⁡ ( τ ∣ X = x i ) / K \varsigma_{i}^{2}=\mathrm{Var}(\tau\mid X=x_{i})/K varies across query points, and is largest precisely where the individual treatment effect is most heterogeneous, so the inflation is heaviest in the regions where posterior width is most informative.

sections.heading: Full objective.
sections.text: To align the point prediction with the estimand, a squared-error penalty on the posterior mean is added, ℒ mean = 1 n q ∑ i = 1 n q ( 𝔼 q θ [ Q ∣ x i , 𝒟 N ] − t i ) 2 , 𝔼 q θ [ Q ∣ x i , 𝒟 N ] = ∑ b = 1 B q θ [ b ∣ x i , 𝒟 N ] c b , \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{mean}}=\frac{1}{n_{q}}\sum_{i=1}^{n_{q}}\Bigl(\mathbb{E}_{q_{\theta}}\bigl[Q\mid x_{i},\mathcal{D}_{N}\bigr]-t_{i}\Bigr)^{2},\qquad\mathbb{E}_{q_{\theta}}\bigl[Q\mid x_{i},\mathcal{D}_{N}\bigr]=\sum_{b=1}^{B}q_{\theta}[b\mid x_{i},\mathcal{D}_{N}]\,c_{b}, (38) with c b = ( e b + e b + 1 ) / 2 c_{b}=(e_{b}+e_{b+1})/2 the bin centers, giving ℒ = ℒ noise ​ _ ​ aware + λ mean ​ ℒ mean \mathcal{L}=\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{noise\_aware}}+\lambda_{\mathrm{mean}}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{mean}} . The penalty does not compete with the distributional objective: because the Monte Carlo error is zero-mean, the minimizer of ( 36 ) already carries the posterior mean and hence minimizes ( 38 ) as well, leaving the population optimum of ℒ \mathcal{L} unchanged for any λ mean ≥ 0 \lambda_{\mathrm{mean}}\geq 0 . At inference time the predictive distribution is reported un-blurred , as q θ ( ⋅ ∣ x ⋆ , 𝒟 N ) q_{\theta}(\cdot\mid x^{\star},\mathcal{D}_{N}) .

sections.heading: Validity of the objective.
sections.text: Three logged diagnostics establish that the loss the curves above report was well posed throughout. First, the grid of the output head is a hard support constraint: a target outside [ v min , v max ] [v_{\min},v_{\max}] cannot be represented by any forecast on the grid, so a non-negligible out-of-grid fraction would invalidate every number scored on it. Averaged over the CATE targets in the on-the-fly synthetic training prior, the share of targets falling outside the grid is 2.0 × 10 − 4 2.0\times 10^{-4} , i.e. 0.02 % 0.02\% , exceeding 1 % 1\% on 275 275 of 75 000 75\,000 steps. Second, the Monte Carlo targets carried their full replicate budget. Each query row’s CATE target is an average over K K replicate draws, and the realized K K can be capped below the requested value by the generator’s memory budget. The mean realized K K was 250 250 — the requested value — at every logged step, so the cap never bound. Third, sampling noise remained material at K = 250 K=250 Monte Carlo replicates. The ratio of the mean target-noise standard deviation ς i \varsigma_{i} to the mean predicted posterior standard deviation averaged 0.20 0.20 , rising from 0.15 0.15 shortly after the anneal to 0.22 0.22 over the final third as the posterior sharpened while ς i ∝ K − 1 / 2 \varsigma_{i}\propto K^{-1/2} remained fixed. Ignoring this noise would therefore add the heterogeneous per-row variance ς i 2 \varsigma_{i}^{2} to the learned posterior variance, motivating the noise-aware correction.

sections.heading: C.3.1 Post-training on larger context sizes
sections.text: The main training run represents contexts of at most 2 048 2\,048 observations. We therefore perform a post-training experiment to test whether the limited support at larger context sizes contributes to the plateau observed in Section 4.2 . Starting from the completed main-training checkpoint, we optimize for a total of 30 000 30\,000 steps on the same causal prior and noise-aware objective, but draw context sizes uniformly from 64 64 to 5 000 5\,000 observations (with 128 128 query rows). Uniform, rather than log-uniform, sampling ensures that the adaptation gives substantial weight to the newly introduced large contexts while retaining smaller contexts for rehearsal. We retain the effective meta-batch size of 64 64 datasets, use a lower learning rate of 2 × 10 − 5 2\times 10^{-5} with a 500 500 -step warmup, and enable activation recomputation to fit the longer sequences. To make this adaptation inexpensive and limit changes to the learned representation, we load the complete main-training checkpoint and freeze all parameters except the in-context predictor. Within that predictor, its first six transformer blocks are frozen as well, so only its later layers and unfrozen predictor parameters are optimized. We evaluate the resulting checkpoints on separate frozen prior and realistic validation suites constructed at large context sizes.

sections.heading: C.4.1 Validation datasets
sections.text: We monitor the training of ProximalFM on a fixed suite of 480 480 datasets, balanced across 12 12 hand-written realistic proximal mechanisms. These mechanisms cover clinical severity and frailty, latent patient subtypes, threshold-based treatment assignment, utilization counts, censored survival, marketing uplift, educational selection, wage returns, hierarchical site effects, nonlinear ordinal proxies, interaction-driven confounding, and near-null effects under strong confounding. These settings span a diverse range of datasets: continuous, binary, ordinal and categorical variables, the treatment is binary, the outcomes may be continuous, skewed, count-valued, zero-inflated, or censored. For each dataset, the dimensions of U U , X X , W W and Z Z are sampled with the same procedure as in the prior ( Section B.2.2 ). Each episode contains exactly 2048 2048 context rows and 128 128 query points. The query target CATEs are computed by averaging 10 000 10\,000 Monte Carlo replicates of ITE draws. At this replicate count, the Monte Carlo sampling noise is approximately 0.025 0.025 times the predictive posterior standard deviation (of the last model checkpoint). The same fixed validation set is evaluated at every training checkpoint.

sections.heading: C.4.2 Point-estimate validation
sections.text: We measure the point-estimate performance at both ATE and CATE levels. The ATE prediction is estimated as the average of the CATE predictions from the query set, ATE ^ = 1 n q ​ ∑ i = 1 n q τ ^ i , \widehat{\mathrm{ATE}}=\frac{1}{n_{q}}\sum_{i=1}^{n_{q}}\hat{\tau}_{i}, and so is the target ATE also computed from the references CATEs. To evaluate the ATE estimation, we use the root mean squared error (RMSE) and the bias of the ATE normalized by the standard deviation of the episode’s CATEs. Regarding CATE evaluation, we use normalized precision in estimation of heterogeneous effect (nPEHE), nPEHE = 1 n q ​ ∑ i = 1 n q ( τ ^ i − τ i ) 2 Var i ​ ( τ i ) . \mathrm{nPEHE}=\sqrt{\frac{\frac{1}{n_{q}}\sum_{i=1}^{n_{q}}(\hat{\tau}_{i}-\tau_{i})^{2}}{\mathrm{Var}_{i}(\tau_{i})}}. (39) We also measure the shape- R 2 R^{2} , which isolates the recovery of treatment-effect heterogeneity from constant level error, R shape 2 = 1 − Var i ​ ( τ ^ i − τ i ) Var i ​ ( τ i ) . R^{2}_{\mathrm{shape}}=1-\frac{\mathrm{Var}_{i}(\hat{\tau}_{i}-\tau_{i})}{\mathrm{Var}_{i}(\tau_{i})}. (40) A constant-ATE prediction gives nPEHE = 1 \mathrm{nPEHE}=1 and R shape 2 = 0 R^{2}_{\mathrm{shape}}=0 . sections.heading: C.4.3 Distributional validation
sections.text: We evaluate the predictive posterior using the continuous ranked probability score (CRPS), the predictive standard deviation relative to the prediction error, and empirical coverage of central credible intervals. For query row i i , let q i q_{i} denote the predicted distribution over Q ⁡ ( x i ) Q(x_{i}) , with CDF F i F_{i} , mean μ i \mu_{i} , and variance v i 2 v_{i}^{2} . Let Q K , i Q_{K,i} denote the Monte Carlo CATE target and let ς i 2 \varsigma_{i}^{2} denote its estimated sampling variance. The CRPS evaluates the full predictive distribution against the target: CRPS ( q i , Q K , i ) = ∫ [ F i ( t ) − 𝟏 { t ≥ Q K , i } ] 2 d t . \operatorname{CRPS}(q_{i},Q_{K,i})=\int\left[F_{i}(t)-\mathbf{1}\{t\geq Q_{K,i}\}\right]^{2}\,\mathrm{d}t. (41) We also report the ratio of predictive standard deviation to prediction error, SD / RMSE = 1 M ​ ∑ i = 1 n q v i 2 1 n q ​ ∑ i = 1 n q ( μ i − Q K , i ) 2 − 1 M ​ ∑ i = 1 n q ς i 2 , \mathrm{SD/RMSE}=\sqrt{\frac{\frac{1}{M}\sum_{i=1}^{n_{q}}v_{i}^{2}}{\frac{1}{n_{q}}\sum_{i=1}^{n_{q}}\left(\mu_{i}-Q_{K,i}\right)^{2}-\frac{1}{M}\sum_{i=1}^{n_{q}}\varsigma_{i}^{2}}}, (42) where n q n_{q} is the total number of validation query rows. The subtraction of ς i 2 \varsigma_{i}^{2} removes the Monte Carlo noise from the observed prediction error. This denominator equals the average predictive variance under calibration, in expectation. Values below one indicate overconfident predictions, whereas values above one indicate underconfidence. Figure C.3 displays the evolution of these distributional metrics during training. sections.heading: C.4.4 Posterior representation & smoothing
sections.text: The histogram representation of the predictive posterior can produce visually spiky densities. Small changes in the allocation of probability across neighbouring bins may have little effect on the training objective while producing noticeably different density shapes. We therefore use the CDF as an intermediate representation for visualization. A Savitzky–Golay filter is applied to the raw CDF, and the corresponding density is obtained by numerical differentiation. As illustrated in Figure C.4 , the smoothed CDF stays very close to the original CDF, but its implied density is easier to interpret. This postprocessing is applied only for visual inspection and does not alter the predictive distribution used to compute validation metrics. sections.heading: D.1.1 Backdoor meta-learners, in-context learners and proxy marginalization
sections.text: We evaluate some methods estimating the CATE under the backdoor adjustment assumptions. First, we evaluat standard causal meta-learners from the backdoor adjustment framework ( Künzel et al., 2019 ) , specifically the S-learner, T-learner, and X-learner. We also implement some in-context learners: CausalPFN ( Balazadeh Meresht et al., 2026 ) , CausalFM ( Ma et al., 2026 ) and Do-PFN ( Robertson et al., 2026 ) . In our proximal causal setting, the presence of the unobserved confounder U U directly violates the conditional ignorability assumption these methods rely on ( Y ⁡ ( a ) ⟂ ⟂ A | X Y(a)\perp\!\!\!\perp A\mid X ). Consequently, all backdoor methods are misspecified. They serve as empirical baselines. Because the causal estimand of interest is the covariate-conditional effect Q ⁡ ( x ) = 𝔼 ⁡ [ Y ⁡ ( 1 ) − Y ⁡ ( 0 ) ∣ X = x ] Q(x)=\mathbb{E}[Y(1)-Y(0)\mid X=x] , yet observational data contain proxy variables ( W , Z ) (W,Z) that carry information about U U , we evaluate backdoor methods under two distinct options: 1. Discard proxies ( X X -only): The learners are trained exclusively on baseline covariates X X , discarding ( W , Z ) (W,Z) entirely. This reflects the standard practice of ignoring unobserved confounding and assuming Y ⁡ ( a ) ⟂ ⟂ A | X Y(a)\perp\!\!\!\perp A\mid X . 2. Proxy conditioning with marginalization ( ( X , W , Z ) → X (X,W,Z)\to X ): To avoid disadvantaging backdoor methods by withholding proxy features, we also fit learners on the full feature set ( X , W , Z ) (X,W,Z) . Because this yields a proxy-conditional effect τ ^ ​ ( x , w , z ) \hat{\tau}(x,w,z) rather than Q ⁡ ( x ) Q(x) , we post-process the predictions by integrating out ( W , Z ) (W,Z) with respect to a local empirical estimate of P ⁡ ( W , Z ∣ X = x ) P(W,Z\mid X=x) . Note that even with proxy features and marginalization, Option 2 does not identify Q ⁡ ( x ) Q(x) : naive regression is insufficient under the proximal assumptions ( Section 2 ).

sections.heading: Meta-learner formulations.
sections.text: We evaluate three meta-learning architectures ( Künzel et al., 2019 ) : • S-Learner: Fits a single regressor μ ^ \hat{\mu} on the pooled data predicting Y Y from features and treatment A A . The effect is estimated as τ ^ S ​ ( x ) = μ ^ ​ ( x , 1 ) − μ ^ ​ ( x , 0 ) \hat{\tau}_{\mathrm{S}}(x)=\hat{\mu}(x,1)-\hat{\mu}(x,0) . When proxies are included, it estimates τ ^ S ​ ( x , w , z ) = μ ^ ​ ( x , 1 , w , z ) − μ ^ ​ ( x , 0 , w , z ) \hat{\tau}_{\mathrm{S}}(x,w,z)=\hat{\mu}(x,1,w,z)-\hat{\mu}(x,0,w,z) . • T-Learner: Fits separate regressors μ ^ 0 \hat{\mu}_{0} on the control cohort ( A = 0 A=0 ) and μ ^ 1 \hat{\mu}_{1} on the treated cohort ( A = 1 A=1 ), predicting τ ^ T = μ ^ 1 − μ ^ 0 \hat{\tau}_{\mathrm{T}}=\hat{\mu}_{1}-\hat{\mu}_{0} . This allows separate response surfaces for each arm, at the cost of not sharing information across arms. • X-Learner: A four-stage crossover architecture designed for imbalanced treatments. After fitting base models μ ^ 0 , μ ^ 1 \hat{\mu}_{0},\hat{\mu}_{1} , it imputes counterfactual pseudo-effects D 1 = Y 1 − μ ^ 0 ​ ( X 1 ) D_{1}=Y_{1}-\hat{\mu}_{0}(X_{1}) and D 0 = μ ^ 1 ​ ( X 0 ) − Y 0 D_{0}=\hat{\mu}_{1}(X_{0})-Y_{0} , trains second-stage models τ ^ 1 \hat{\tau}_{1} and τ ^ 0 \hat{\tau}_{0} to predict them, and combines them using an estimated propensity score e ^ \hat{e} : τ ^ X = e ^ ​ τ ^ 0 + ( 1 − e ^ ) ​ τ ^ 1 . \hat{\tau}_{\mathrm{X}}=\hat{e}\,\hat{\tau}_{0}+(1-\hat{e})\,\hat{\tau}_{1}. (43) In our implementation, e ^ \hat{e} is estimated via logistic regression. Each meta-learner accepts three distinct base model classes: • Ridge regression: Standardized linear model with penalty α ∈ { 0.1 , 1 , 10 , 100 , 1000 } \alpha\in\{0.1,1,10,100,1000\} selected via 4-fold cross-validation. • Random forest: 100 trees with maximum depth ∈ { 1 , 3 , 5 } \in\{1,3,5\} and minimum leaf size ∈ { 1 , 5 , 10 } \in\{1,5,10\} chosen via 4-fold cross-validation. • TabICLv2 ( Qu et al., 2026 ) : In-context tabular foundation model evaluated zero-shot.

sections.heading: In-context learners.
sections.text: We evaluate CausalPFN, CausalFM and Do-PFN in their pretrained, zero-shot form: each model uses the episode’s observed data as context, with no episode-specific parameter updates. CausalPFN and CausalFM directly return a CATE prediction for each query. Do-PFN instead predicts outcomes under each treatment arm, and we take their difference to form the CATE.

sections.heading: Proxy marginalization.
sections.text: When trained on ( X , W , Z ) (X,W,Z) , a meta-learner predicts a proxy-conditional contrast τ ^ ​ ( x , w , z ) \hat{\tau}(x,w,z) . Because the evaluation target is the covariate-conditional effect Q ⁡ ( x ) = 𝔼 ⁡ [ Y ⁡ ( 1 ) − Y ⁡ ( 0 ) ∣ X = x ] Q(x)=\mathbb{E}[Y(1)-Y(0)\mid X=x] , we recover a function of x x alone by integrating out the proxies against a local empirical estimate of P ⁡ ( W , Z ∣ X = x ) P(W,Z\mid X=x) : τ ^ ​ ( x ) = ∑ i ∈ 𝒩 k ​ ( x ) q i ​ ( x ) ​ τ ^ ​ ( x , W i , Z i ) . \hat{\tau}(x)=\sum_{i\in\mathcal{N}_{k}(x)}q_{i}(x)\,\hat{\tau}(x,W_{i},Z_{i}). (44) Crucially, the integration uses the aligned context pairs ( W i , Z i ) (W_{i},Z_{i}) rather than a Cartesian product of marginals, preserving the empirical joint dependence between the two proxies. The neighborhood 𝒩 k ​ ( x ) \mathcal{N}_{k}(x) comprises the k k context points closest to x x under a feature-standardized Euclidean distance: d ⁡ ( x , X i ) = ∑ d = 1 d X ( x d − X i , d ) 2 σ d 2 , σ d = 2 ​ median j , l ​ ( | X j , d − X l , d | ) . d(x,X_{i})=\sqrt{\sum_{d=1}^{d_{X}}\frac{(x_{d}-X_{i,d})^{2}}{\sigma_{d}^{2}}},\qquad\sigma_{d}=\sqrt{2}\,\mathrm{median}_{j,l}\big(|X_{j,d}-X_{l,d}|\big). (45) We evaluate two local weighting schemes for q i ​ ( x ) q_{i}(x) : • k k -NN weighting: Uniform weights over the k k nearest context atoms, q i ​ ( x ) = 1 / k q_{i}(x)=1/k . • Gaussian kernel weighting: Nadaraya-Watson exponential weights with bandwidth scale s > 0 s>0 : q i ​ ( x ) = exp ( − ( d ( x , X i ) 2 − min j ∈ 𝒩 k ​ ( x ) d ( x , X j ) 2 ) / s ) ∑ l ∈ 𝒩 k ​ ( x ) exp ( − ( d ( x , X l ) 2 − min j ∈ 𝒩 k ​ ( x ) d ( x , X j ) 2 ) / s ) . q_{i}(x)=\frac{\exp\big(-\big(d(x,X_{i})^{2}-\min_{j\in\mathcal{N}_{k}(x)}d(x,X_{j})^{2}\big)/s\big)}{\sum_{l\in\mathcal{N}_{k}(x)}\exp\big(-\big(d(x,X_{l})^{2}-\min_{j\in\mathcal{N}_{k}(x)}d(x,X_{j})^{2}\big)/s\big)}. (46) In our benchmarks, we use k = 16 k=16 and fixed kernel scale s = 1.0 s=1.0 .

sections.heading: D.1.2 P-learner
sections.text: We implement the P-learner of Sverdrup and Cui (2023) . The cross-fitted score and final-stage regression follow their procedure. For bridge estimation, we use a Nyström-approximation of the minimax RKHS formulation, described below. For each data point, we compute the doubly robust proximal score: Γ i = ( − 1 ) 1 − A i ​ q ​ ( Z i , A i , X i ) ​ ( Y i − h ⁡ ( W i , A i , X i ) ) + h ⁡ ( W i , 1 , X i ) − h ⁡ ( W i , 0 , X i ) , \Gamma_{i}=(-1)^{1-A_{i}}\,q(Z_{i},A_{i},X_{i})\big(Y_{i}-h(W_{i},A_{i},X_{i})\big)+h(W_{i},1,X_{i})-h(W_{i},0,X_{i}), (47) The outcome and treatment bridges are characterized, for a ∈ { 0 , 1 } a\in\{0,1\} , by the conditional moments 𝔼 [ 𝟏 { A = a } { Y − h ( W , a , X ) } ∣ Z , X ] = 0 , 𝔼 [ 𝟏 { A = a } q ( Z , a , X ) − 1 ∣ W , X ] = 0 . \begin{split}\mathbb{E}\!\left[\mathbf{1}\{A=a\}\{Y-h(W,a,X)\}\mid Z,X\right]&=0,\\ \mathbb{E}\!\left[\mathbf{1}\{A=a\}q(Z,a,X)-1\mid W,X\right]&=0.\end{split} (48) We obtain the CATE estimate by regressing the cross-fitted scores on X X , Q ^ ​ ( x ) = 𝔼 ^ ​ [ Γ ^ ∣ X = x ] \hat{Q}(x)=\hat{\mathbb{E}}[\hat{\Gamma}\mid X=x] . The mean of the same scores gives the corresponding proximal ATE estimate.

sections.heading: Kernel bridge estimation.
sections.text: We estimate both bridges using the regularised minimax RKHS formulation of Dikkala et al. (2020) , following Sverdrup and Cui (2023) . The outcome bridge h h is represented by RBF features Φ H \Phi_{H} of ( W , X ) (W,X) , and the treatment bridge q q by Φ Q \Phi_{Q} of ( Z , X ) (Z,X) . Because of computational and memory constraints, we use the Nyström method with r r landmark points sampled from the training fold. The kernel bridge estimators have closed-form solutions with penalties λ h \lambda_{h} and λ q \lambda_{q} on the two bridges.

sections.heading: Hyperparameter tuning.
sections.text: Several components of the method is subject to a choice of parameter. First of all, the CATE predictor Q ^ ( . ) \hat{Q}(.) can be made using any general predictor. We use a ridge regularized linear regression, a random forest or TabICL ( Qu et al., 2026 ) . The parameters of the random forest and ridge regressor are chosen by cross-validation, TabICL does not require parameter tuning. Then, regarding the bridge functions h h and q q , the regularizer λ h \lambda_{h} and λ q \lambda_{q} are chosen by cross-validation to minimize their moment loss. The Nyström rank r r is fixed. The kernel bandwidth is chosen by the median heuristic, and not searched. Table D.2 summarizes the hyperparameters.

sections.heading: D.1.3 Neural moment matching regression
sections.text: We adapted the implementation of the neural moment matching regression (NMMR) method of Kompa et al. (2022) 2 2 2 Original implementation available at https://github.com/beamlab-hsph/Neural-Moment-Matching-Regression . to our setting. Their code estimates one population-level quantity per dataset, 𝔼 ⁡ [ Y ∣ do ⁡ ( A = a ) ] \mathbb{E}[Y\mid\mathrm{do}(A=a)] , evaluated on a grid of treatment values, which for a binary treatment is simply the two arms whose difference is the ATE. Our benchmark instead asks for the CATE Q ^ ​ ( x ) \hat{Q}(x) at each query row of every episode.

sections.heading: The method.
sections.text: NMMR replaces the outcome bridge h 0 h_{0} of ( 2 ) by a neural network g ϕ ​ ( x , w , a ) ∈ ℝ g_{\phi}(x,w,a)\in\mathbb{R} and fits it directly, with no two-stage regression. This neural network is trained on an observational dataset, with simple gradient descent. It uses the following loss function, determined by an RBF kernel matrix on the conditioning variables A A , Z Z and X X : r i = Y i − g ϕ ​ ( X i , W i , A i ) , K i ​ j = exp ⁡ ( − ‖ κ i − κ j ‖ 2 2 ​ ℓ 2 ) , κ i = ( A i , Z i / σ ^ Z , X i / σ ^ X ) , r_{i}=Y_{i}-g_{\phi}(X_{i},W_{i},A_{i}),\qquad K_{ij}=\exp\!\Big(-\tfrac{\left\lVert\kappa_{i}-\kappa_{j}\right\rVert^{2}}{2\ell^{2}}\Big),\quad\kappa_{i}=\big(A_{i},\;Z_{i}/\hat{\sigma}_{Z},\;X_{i}/\hat{\sigma}_{X}\big), (49) which determines the quadratic forms to minimize R ^ V = r ⊤ ​ K ​ r n 2 or R ^ U = r ⊤ ​ ( K − diag ​ ( K ) ) ​ r n ⁡ ( n − 1 ) , \hat{R}_{V}=\frac{r^{\top}K\,r}{n^{2}}\qquad\text{or}\qquad\hat{R}_{U}=\frac{r^{\top}\big(K-\mathrm{diag}(K)\big)\,r}{n(n-1)}, (50) the V- and U-statistics. The U-statistic drops the diagonal: it is unbiased but noisier, while the V-statistic is biased but lower variance. We report both as separate entries, as in the original paper.

sections.heading: Deviations at prediction time.
sections.text: The reference code never produces a conditional ATE, even though the bridge it fits supports one. It returns a single scalar per arm, 𝔼 W , X ​ [ g ϕ ​ ( a , W , X ) ] \mathbb{E}_{W,X}[g_{\phi}(a,W,X)] , whose difference is an ATE. Recovering Q ⁡ ( x ) Q(x) of ( 3 ) instead means marginalising W W at each query point ; we consider two possibilities. 1. We assume W ⟂ ⟂ X W\perp\!\!\!\perp X (“ind. W”). The direct transposition of the reference code: average the fitted bridge over the empirical marginal of W W in the context, Q ^ ​ ( x ) = 1 n ​ ∑ i g ϕ ​ ( x , W i , 1 ) − g ϕ ​ ( x , W i , 0 ) \hat{Q}(x)=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i}g_{\phi}(x,W_{i},1)-g_{\phi}(x,W_{i},0) . This is a valid strategy only if one assumes that W ⟂ ⟂ X W\perp\!\!\!\perp X . 2. We do not assume W ⟂ ⟂ X W\perp\!\!\!\perp X (“cond. W”). We approximate 𝔼 ⁡ [ g ϕ ​ ( x , W , a ) ∣ X = x ] \mathbb{E}[g_{\phi}(x,W,a)\mid X=x] by averaging over the marginal of W W implied by the context, reweighted by a Gaussian kernel on X X . This computes the proximal g-formula, without independence assumption, but at a cost of an extra smoothing bandwidth.

sections.heading: Implementation corrections & computational notes.
sections.text: We do the following changes in the code compared to original code. First, in the MLP used to model the bridge function, the original implementation applied a ReLU transformation on the last layer. This made the prediction of negative outcomes impossible, and was removed in our implementation. Second, for computational optimization, we avoid recomputing the kernel matrix at each iteration mini-batch, but compute the complete matrix once and sub-sample from it.

sections.heading: Kernel bandwidth.
sections.text: The original implementation uses a fixed bandwidth of l = 1.0 l=1.0 in the Equation 49 . This has obvious drawbacks as the average distance between data points grow with the dimensionality of these points. In non-trivial dimensions, the kernel becomes the identity matrix, and all information from the proxy Z Z is lost: the bridge function becomes a direct estimator of Y Y in the V-statistic case, and very unstable in the U-statistic one. Therefore, we implement an alternative bandwidth which is defined by the median heuristic and does not suffer from this degeneration in higher dimension. Both alternatives are evaluated.

(52) Here λ \lambda penalises ‖ h ‖ ℋ L \left\lVert h\right\rVert_{\mathcal{H}_{L}} and is the regulariser of the original method; ϵ \epsilon is added for numerical stability.

sections.text: We reimplemented the kernel proxy variable (KPV) method of Mastouri et al. (2021) , presented in the same paper as PMMR and sharing its released code. Again, the reimplementation allowed us to adjust the code for our usage: binary kernel and CATE predictions.

sections.heading: Hyperparameter selection.
sections.text: We use the authors’ closed-form leave-one-out criterion for both regularisers, run inside each fit. On the other hand, we modify the hyperparameter tuning of the kernel bandwidth. As suggested by the authors, we initialize the search by the median heuristic. We then search around this initialization by minimizing the stage-2 leave-one-out criterion (instead of the stage-1 one, used in their implementation). We prefer this as it compares bandwidths using prediction error against the same outcome Y Y , whereas stage-1 LOOCV changes both the input kernel and the W W -kernel defining the loss, making scores across bandwidths less directly comparable. Table D.5 summarises the tuning parameters.

sections.heading: D.3.1 Speed
sections.text: We measured runtime in a separate run of the 36 semi-synthetic episodes with nonlinear mechanisms, strong confounding, and weak proxy information. Episodes were executed sequentially in one process to avoid contention between simultaneous benchmark jobs; methods retained the parallelism specified for their own hyperparameter searches. At each context size, the recorded wall-clock time covers estimator construction, fitting, and prediction on the 256 query rows. The filled points in Figure 5 show the median of these per-episode times at n ctx = 2 048 n_{\mathrm{ctx}}=2\,048 ; hollow points subtract the measured hyperparameter-search time. Accuracy ranks come independently from the complete semi-synthetic evaluation matrix, using paired episode-level CATE nPEHE ranks.

sections.heading: D.4 Synthetic study of proxy informativeness
sections.text: We vary proxy information within a fixed causal mechanism to examine when proximal estimation offers an advantage over regression adjustment using proxies. For each d ∈ { 1 , 3 , 5 } d\in\{1,3,5\} , we generate 20 20 information levels equally spaced from 0.01 0.01 to 0.99 0.99 . For each of the resulting 60 60 datasets, we evaluate methods using 128 128 , 512 512 , or 2 048 2\,048 context rows and the same 256 256 held-out query rows. sections.heading: Discussion.
sections.text: Figure D.4 shows the advantage of a well-specified proximal estimator: the 2SLS bridge basis contains the true outcome bridge. Its large fluctuations at low proxy information reflect the difficulty of estimating that bridge with weak instruments, rather than model misspecification. ProximalFM improves more smoothly as information increases and, at n ctx = 2 048 n_{\mathrm{ctx}}=2\,048 , outperforms proxy-marginalized CausalPFN throughout the sweep and proxy-adjusted OLS in most settings. OLS is a favourable comparator here: the treatment effect is linear, and independence of X X and ( W , Z ) (W,Z) makes proxy marginalisation a simple average over context rows, without conditional-neighbour estimation. As the proxies nearly reveal U U , OLS catches up with and surpasses ProximalFM . These curves come from one paired simulation per setting.

sections.heading: Appendix E Towards a real physical system: Causal Chambers
sections.text: We use the Light Tunnel Mk2 on the Causal Chamber platform 5 5 5 See https://causalchamber.ai for more details. ( Gamella et al., 2025 ; Zeitler, 2025 ) to study average treatment effects in a controllable but real (non-simulated) optical system. The experiment combines physical responses with software control to create dependence between a hidden confounder, proxy variables, treatment, and outcome. This provides an exploratory step towards proximal estimation in a real-world systems, complementing the synthetic CATE benchmarks. sections.heading: Physical setup and causal structure.
sections.text: Figure E.1 shows the physical setup with the variables we consider, and Figure E.2 shows the intended pathways between them. The confounder U U is an LED drive drawn uniformly from the integers 0 , … , 255 0,\ldots,255 , controlling its brightness. The observed covariate X X controls a red LED, Z Z controls the ultraviolet LED 2, and W W controls the position (in degrees) of the first polariser. Treatment A ∈ { 0 , 1 } A\in\{0,1\} sets ultraviolet LED 3 to drive a 1 ​ A a_{1}A , and the outcome Y Y is the infrared sensor 3 reading. Auxiliary measurements comprise the electrical current C C drawn by the confounder LED, infrared readings I 1 , I 2 I_{1},I_{2} , and visible-light reading V 1 V_{1} . The pathways C → X C\to X , I 1 → Z I_{1}\to Z , V 1 → W V_{1}\to W , and I 2 → A I_{2}\to A —resulting from the software control functions—link successive physical measurements to subsequent interventions.
